title: Subqueries and CTEs

spans.text: “Subqueries and CTEs” is a tool for solving a concrete programming problem. Identify the input and desired result, then trace what role the construct plays in the example. Study it not only as syntax, but also for its effects on readability, correctness, resource use, and future changes.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
The first query selects students with at least one enrollment; the recursive CTE generates numbers from 1 through 5.

A subquery runs inside another query; a correlated subquery can refer to a value from the outer row. EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns at least one row and is useful for finding related records. A CTE names an intermediate result with WITH, while WITH RECURSIVE can walk hierarchies step by step. A CTE usually exists only for that statement; it is not automatically a stored table.

Key line: `SELECT s.name`
What it does: The first query selects students with at least one enrollment; the recursive CTE generates numbers from 1 through 5.
Why it is used: Give each CTE a meaningful name and inspect intermediate results one step at a time.
If omitted or changed: A CTE can improve readability, but it is not guaranteed to be faster on every database.

spans.text: CTE and subquery performance depends on the engine and optimizer; inspect large workloads with EXPLAIN.
